body.text: As 2026 approaches its final stretch, The Diplomat’s editors wanted to share some of our favorite books. Most are non-fiction and come from years past, but each finds extended relevance in the twists and turns of the past year.
Need a gift for a Diplomat reader? Start with our Editors’ Favorites, or check out books that have been featured – through interviews and articles – on The Diplomat.
Buy any book through our Bookshop.org shop and The Diplomat gets a small cut of the price.
Shannon Tiezzi, Editor-in-Chief

It’s no secret that China’s government is using new technologies to surveil its people – and shape their actions as needed. In this book, WSJ journalists Josh Chin and Liza Lin outline exactly how this transformation has occurred. It’s a masterful treatment of one of the most consequential developments in China today: how digital technologies went from a potential threat to the CCP’s absolute rule to the primary instrument of social control.

Longtime China watcher Ian Johnson’s book offers a useful counterpoint to Chin and Lin’s treatment of the surveillance. “Sparks” profiles the voices of resistance that still very much exist in today’s China, through the example of “underground historians” – people who refuse to accept the CCP’s sanitized rewriting of deeply traumatic episodes like the Great Famine and the Cultural Revolution. The book is both a human portrait of specific people and a hopeful exploration of the limits of state control – despite the rapid advent of technology.
Bonus: Read Tiezzi’s interview with Ian Johnson here.
Catherine Putz, Managing Editor

Ten years after the 2016 death of Uzbekistan’s first president, Islam Karimov, the country’s persona on the world stage has changed dramatically. But as journalist Joanna Lillis chronicles in “Silk Mirage,” the old and the new are intertwined in modern Uzbekistan, a tapestry woven of opportunity and struggle, of fear and hope. What “Silk Mirage” doesn’t do is pass judgement. Instead, Lillis gives space to the full spectrum of voices from inside Uzbekistan and leaves it to the reader to sort through what that complexity ultimately means, what they see in the flickering of the mirage on the horizon.
Bonus: Read Putz’s interview with Lillis here.

In this speculative novel, a disillusioned Kazakh molecular biologist clones Kenesary, the last khan of the Kazakh Khanate. At 18, young Kenesary moves to London for school where he meets a Uyghur named Abdullah who, with the help of an AI assistant during his “internship” in Xinjiang, realized he’s the reincarnation of Amursana, the last Jungar prince. Together, Kenesary and Abdullah decide to petition the British Queen to recognize their royal status but they run into trouble from both a Russian agent and the Kazakh president. Not everything is what it seems. Can they revive the nomadic ways as Kenesary’s father intended? Do they even really want to?

In the ways only fiction can, Bekakhmetov’s novella poses challenging questions about identity and intent; wraps them in a uniquely Kazakh brand of sardonic humor and sets them free in an absurdist tale that couldn’t be told in any other way.
Sebastian Strangio, Southeast Asia Editor

In late 1941 and early 1942, the armies of imperial Japan launched a surprise invasion of Britain’s colonies in Malaya and Burma. The lightning campaign culminated in the devastating fall of Singapore – a city that Winston Churchill believed impregnable – in just 55 days. In this rich narrative history, Bayly and Harper describe the host of obscure resistance forces that emerged across Southeast Asia during the war – and how the Japanese occupation shaped the politics of postcolonial Asia.
“Embers of War: The Fall of an Empire and the Making of America’s Vietnam,” by Fredrik Logevall

In this Pulitzer Prize-winning book, Fredrik Logevall narrates the decomposition and collapse of French colonial rule in Indochina, and the crucial years that marked the run-up to the U.S. intervention in Vietnam. Through a close familiarity with French, American, and Vietnamese sources, “Embers of War” reveals how the incipient Cold War shifted American leaders’ perceptions of Ho Chi Minh’s communists, and put the U.S. on a path to replicating the French failure in Vietnam.
Sudha Ramachandran, South Asia Editor

Sam Dalrymple’s Shattered Lands takes readers beyond the well-known partition of 1947 to explore the five great partitions that shaped modern Asia. A mere century ago, the political unit known as India encompassed a far greater territory and population than the modern nation-state of India. Dalrymple explores how this polity gave rise to a number of new nations and why they were separated from India, ranging from Burma to Yemen to the princely states to Pakistan.

Pegged on the deadly military clashes between Indian and Chinese soldiers at Galwan in Ladakh in June 2020, “Understanding the India-China Border” is a historical account of the seven decades of failed attempts to find a negotiated settlement to the India-China border dispute. Through anecdotes and conversations with key actors in India and China, Manoj Joshi tells the story of how the two countries not only fought wars and near-wars in the high Himalayas but also reached agreements and put in place a peace of sorts along the disputed border.
